findings.quote: One trip takes about $365.24$ days, which is why a calendar year needs leap days.
findings.problem: The lesson gives the wrong year for one trip around the Sun. One full orbit, measured against the stars, is the sidereal year: about 365.256 days. The figure 365.24 is the seasonal (tropical) year, from one March equinox to the next. That year is about 20 minutes shorter because of precession. The lesson repeats the error in 'Earth's trip takes about $365.24$ days' (Leap Years) and 'very close to the real $365.24$'. The leap-year reasoning depends on it: 'Adding a day every fourth year is slightly too much' holds only for the seasonal year, which the calendar follows. For the orbit, 365.256 is more than 365.25, so one leap day every four years would be too few, not too much. The base had this right ('A seasonal (tropical) year is about $365.24$ days'), and the rewrite cut that correct teaching.
